chapter_theme: Kudhambai Siddhar's kannis, each a single question to a woman called Kudhambai: for one who has reached a certain state, what need is there of a certain thing? The things dismissed are the instruments of religion and of the Siddhars' own craft: title-deeds, kalpa drugs, mudras, mantras, the hexagon, tantra, diet rules, palanquins, hand-cymbals, and at the top of the list yoga and jnana themselves. The states that make them needless are seeing the open space as truth, sleeplessness with awareness, the crown passed, the deathless walk, bliss welling up. The song is a ladder whose every rung is kicked away once stood on.
structure_note: Every stanza has the same shape: a condition in the first line, the question ஏதுக்கடி with its object in the second, and the refrain குதம்பாய் with the question repeated. The pairs are often rhymed opposites (பட்டயம்/வெட்டவெளி, முக்கோணம்/சட்கோணம், அட்டாங்கம்/முட்டாங்கம், யோகம்/வேகம்). No order is visible beyond a drift from possessions (1575) through ritual instruments (1580 to 1592) to yoga and knowledge (1589, 1595, 1596) and back to festivity (1599).

1575.reading: For those who hold the open space to be the truth, what need of a title-deed?
1575.nuance: பட்டயம் is the copper-plate or palm-leaf deed of ownership; the one whose truth is the open expanse owns nothing bounded enough to deed. The whole song's method is set here: a state named, a document made absurd by it.

1576.reading: For the true jnani who has seen the true thing and shines, what need of kalpa drugs?
1576.nuance: கற்பங்கள், the rejuvenating preparations of the medical Siddhars for a long life, are dismissed by one of their own: the knower has no body-span to prolong. The stanza does not deny that they work, only that the jnani needs them.

1577.reading: For those who see without seeing and stay with attention, what need of vain desire?
1577.nuance: காணாமல் கண்டு, seeing unseen or seeing without the eye, is the Siddhars' phrase for inner sight; கருத்தோடு இருப்போர், those who stay with their attention, recurs in 1599 and is the song's name for the settled knower.

1578.reading: For those who have shed deceit and seen the way, what need of agitation?
1578.nuance: The only stanza whose dismissed thing is a feeling rather than an instrument. Deceit and agitation are paired as cause and effect: the one who has nothing to hide has nothing to fear.

1579.reading: For those who have seen the foundation, foot to crown, what need of disputation?
1579.nuance: அடிமுடி recalls the Lord whose foot and crown Vishnu and Brahma could not find; in the yogic reading it is the row of supports (ஆதாரம்) from the base to the crown, seen in the body. வாதாட்டம் is dispute, but in a Siddhar's mouth வாதம் also means alchemy, and 'what need of alchemy's play' is a possible second sense.

1580.reading: For those who have lost sleep and stay in remembrance, what need of a mudra?
1580.nuance: நித்திரை கெட்டு, sleep destroyed, is the yogic wakefulness that Sivavakkiyar calls sleeping without sleeping; the seals of yoga, which aim at that state, are needless once it is held.

1581.reading: For those who stand in the place that is tantra, what need of mantra?
1581.nuance: தந்திரமான தலம், the place that is technique or that technique reaches, is unexplained; tradition takes it as the inner station the practice brings one to, so that the formula that led there is spent. 1588 goes a step further and dismisses tantra too.

1582.reading: For those who stay in true tapas, what need of contrivance?
1582.nuance: உத்தியம் is unclear: உத்தி, a device or stratagem, is the likeliest root, so 'contrivance'; உத்தியோகம், an occupation, is another reading, giving 'what need of a livelihood'. Either way tapas is set against calculation.

1583.reading: For those who hold to the gaze and reach the one in the middle, what need of wasting away?
1583.nuance: நடுவணை, the middle, is read by tradition as the central channel or its opening, reached by fixing the gaze; it may equally be the Lord who stands in the middle of all. வாட்டங்கள், wastings, may be the body's withering in austerity, so the stanza would say the inward path spares what outward tapas costs.

1584.reading: For the true jnani who has learned the three Tamils and embraces, what need of sounds?
1584.nuance: முத்தமிழ் is Tamil in its three branches, prose, music and drama. The stanza does not set learning against silence; it makes silence the end of learning, which is Tirumular's order too.

1585.reading: For those who have gone above the crown and seen the high space, what need of wishing for anything here?
1585.nuance: உச்சிக்கு மேல், above the crown of the head, is the Siddhars' summit of the body-cosmos; the space seen past it makes 'here' (இங்கு) a place with nothing worth wishing for.

1586.reading: For those cooked without being burnt, who have seen the plain open space, what need of the darkness of delusion?
1586.nuance: வேகாமல் வெந்து, cooked without burning, is coded: tradition hears the body ripened by the inner fire of yoga without being consumed, the alchemists' own figure for the perfected body. மோகாந்தம் is read as மோக அந்தம், the blind end of infatuation; the stanza says only that the ripened one is past it.

1587.reading: For those who have leapt across without dying and walk a solitary way, what need of solitude?
1587.nuance: A paradox: the one on the lone road needs no seclusion, because solitude is a state, not a place. சாகாமல் தாண்டி, crossing without dying, is the Siddhars' claim of a deathless passage, stated and not explained.

1588.reading: For the freed ones who sway and dance in the inner sky, what need of tantra?
1588.nuance: அந்தரம் is the sky or the interval within; the dancing freed ones are a figure for the state beyond practice. Where 1581 kept the place that tantra reaches and dismissed mantra, this stanza dismisses the technique itself, the next rung up.

1589.reading: For those who stay with awareness, bliss welling up, what need of jnana itself?
1589.nuance: The sharpest stanza in the song: ஞானம், the liberating knowledge, is dismissed in its turn, with தான் (itself) marking the surprise. The one in bliss and awareness does not need the knowledge that was the way to them, so jnana is treated as a means, like the mudra and the mantra.

1590.reading: For those who see the painted hall day after day, what need of a charm?
1590.nuance: சித்தரக் கூடம், the picture hall, is read by tradition as the body or the inner place where the picture of the Lord is seen; it could also be the assembly of the siddhas. பத்திரம் is a document, a leaf, or a protective charm; the pairing with 1575's title-deed suggests a written thing, perhaps a horoscope or a deed of safety.

1591.reading: For the true jnani who has sprouted in the triangle, what need of the hexagon?
1591.nuance: Both figures are yantra shapes and body-places. Tradition takes the triangle as the root centre or the goddess's triangle in which the power is born, and the six-cornered figure as the drawn chakra of worship or the heart centre; the stanza says that the one born within needs no drawn diagram.

1592.reading: For the Lord who sways and dances in all eight directions, what need of a dance-stage?
1592.nuance: நாதர் may be the Lord or the master, the siddha; நட்டணை is obscure, perhaps a dancing-place or a set dance. The one stanza whose subject is not a kind of person: the all-pervading dancer needs no hall, which reads as a side-glance at Chidambaram.

1593.reading: For the true jnani who has gained release and whose heart embraces it, what need of diet rules?
1593.nuance: பத்தியம், the regimen prescribed with Siddha medicine, is dismissed as 1576's kalpa was: the medical practice of the Siddhars is for the body of one who still needs curing. The near-rhyme of பத்தியம் with பத்தி, devotion, is probably a deliberate tease.

1594.reading: For those who have removed trouble and stay with awareness, what need of a palanquin?
1594.nuance: The palanquin is the honour carried for the great; the song counts it among the things the knower is above, with the title-deed and the celebration, so the list is not only of religious instruments.

1595.reading: For the true jnani who knows eight-limbed yoga, what need of the eight-limbed prostration?
1595.nuance: முட்டாங்கம் is unexplained; read here as the prostration on knees (முட்டு) and limbs, punning on அட்டாங்கம், so that the inner eightfold discipline replaces the outer eightfold bow. Another reading hears முட்டு as obstruction, 'what obstacle is there'. The next stanza dismisses yoga itself.

1596.reading: For the true jnani who has restrained the rush and shines, what need of yoga itself?
1596.nuance: வேகம், speed or rush, is taken by tradition as the breath's or the mind's; stilling it is what yoga is for, so the one who has done it needs no yoga. With 1589 on jnana, this is the song's doctrine: the practices are scaffolding.

1597.reading: For those who have conquered the great elephant and sit on the mountain, what need of a gift of land?
1597.nuance: மாத்தானை may be the great rutting elephant, a usual figure for the mind or the ego, or the great army; the mountain is the ascetic's seat, or in the body-reading the crown. பூத்தானம் is read as பூதானம், the gift of land to a Brahmin or a temple, which pairs with 1575's deed; it could also be பூ + ஸ்தானம், a place of flowers, or flower-offering.

1598.reading: For the true jnani who wanders like the dead, what need of hand-cymbals?
1598.nuance: The hand-cymbals are the bhajan's instrument; the knower who walks as a corpse has no song to keep time for. The dead-while-living jnani is Tirumular's and Sivavakkiyar's figure, used here with a comic edge.

1599.reading: For those who look on whoever they see and stay with attention, what need of celebration?
1599.nuance: கண்டாரை நோக்கி, looking at those seen, is taken as even regard for all who come; it could also mean watching those who have seen, the realised. கொண்டாட்டம், festivity, is the thing dismissed, where Kaduveli (1561) promised daily கொண்டாட்டம் to the one who gazes heavenward.

links.note: Pattiragiriyar asks when he will see the bare void in the open space and become clear; Kudhambai asks what a title-deed is to those who hold the open space as truth. For both the வெட்டவெளி is the real; Kudhambai draws the consequence for ownership.

Sivavakkiyar describes frauds who smoke and eat drugs so as to be esteemed as kaya-kalpa men; Kudhambai asks what kalpa drugs are to the jnani who has seen the true thing. Sivavakkiyar attacks the pretenders, Kudhambai sets the drugs below knowledge even when genuine; both place the medical craft outside the goal.

Pattiragiriyar asks when he will sleep without sleeping and gain bliss; Kudhambai asks what a mudra is to those who have lost sleep and stay in remembrance. The same wakeful state; Kudhambai adds that the seals of yoga are needless once it is reached.

Tirumular says that with the shambhavi and khechari seals joined, the great Siva-state is the gain of the eight siddhis; Kudhambai asks what a mudra is to the sleepless and aware. The conflict holds on the reading that Tirumular's seals are the means to the state and Kudhambai's aware one is in it; it dissolves if Kudhambai only means the seals are spent after use, which is her method throughout.

Pattinathar describes the guru's teaching as a chakra not drawn, a mantra not spoken, a lingam not built, a puja within thought that does not fail; Kudhambai asks what a mantra is to those who stand in the place of tantra. Both make the inner station replace the spoken formula.

Kaduveli tells the mind to climb the path of true knowledge and be clear in the open space; Kudhambai asks what jnana itself is to those in bliss and awareness. Not a contradiction if jnana is the path and bliss the arrival, but Kudhambai's stanza marks the point at which Kaduveli's counsel runs out.

The Agasthiyar verse places the fire in the triangle and in the six, two and eight, and makes the jiva the five letters; Kudhambai asks what the hexagon is to the jnani sprouted in the triangle. Both use the triangle as the place of origin in the body; Agasthiyar keeps the six as a further station, Kudhambai dismisses it.

Kaduveli tells the mind to discern the incomparable eight-limbed yoga well and know it; Kudhambai asks what the eightfold prostration is to the jnani who knows eight-limbed yoga. Both commend ashtanga as something to know; Kudhambai's next stanza (1596) then dismisses yoga itself, which Kaduveli does not.

Pattiragiriyar asks when he will reach the thing beyond eight-limbed yoga and beyond what lies beyond it; Kudhambai asks what yoga itself is to the jnani who has restrained the rush. Both place the goal past yoga; Pattiragiriyar as a longing, Kudhambai as an arrival already made.

Tirumular says the Siva-gnanis wander as men dead while body and senses remain, unlike the ritual purifiers and the monkey-glad knowers; Kudhambai asks what hand-cymbals are to the jnani who wanders like the dead. The same figure of the corpse-walker; Kudhambai turns it on the bhajan singers, Tirumular on ritualists and false knowers.

Pattiragiriyar asks when, having seen the Father's dwelling, he will wander daily like a dead corpse; Kudhambai asks what hand-cymbals are to the jnani who wanders like the dead. Both make the corpse-walk the knower's outward form after the inner finding.

Kaduveli promises that daily celebration will come on earth to the one who sets his gaze on the heavenly state; Kudhambai asks what celebration is to those who stay with attention. The two uses of கொண்டாட்டம் differ, inner gladness in Kaduveli and festivity in Kudhambai, so the stanzas rub rather than clash.

source_issues: 1585: இச்சிப்பிங்கு runs இச்சிப்பு and இங்கு together; the word division is editorial.
1595: முட்டாங்கம் and 1597: பூத்தானம் are not standard forms and may be corrupt or deliberate puns.
